utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasiljevic, you better come back to the witness box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Domazet: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic, the day before yesterday, we adjourned at about the time when you told us about your stay in Uzice, that is, when you were transferred to the psychiatric ward. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stayed in that ward until when; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 28th of July. That's what the discharge papers say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were released from the orthopedic ward, were you wearing a plastic cast on the injured leg?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up to the knee or above the knee?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to the hip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were discharged from the hospital, that is, from both -- from the psychiatry too, were you still wearing a cast?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the extension of my leg, and that took 21 days, a plastic cast was applied to my leg and I was told that I had to wear it for two months. And they put a plastic cast up to my hip, and 45 days later they shortened it below the knee, that is, a so-called plaster boot, as they call it. So after 45 days, they cut it down below the knee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you move around during that time?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: On crutches. That is, only with the help of the crutches. Otherwise, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend checkups either in Visegrad or in Uzice?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was from Visegrad that I went to have this plastic cast shortened and for the checkup, to Visegrad; that is, I had to report to the general practitioner, then he would give me a paper to go to the specialist, and the treatment was based on the advice of specialists in Uzice. They were responsible for the treatment. And the specialist then wrote to the general practitioner in Visegrad when I was to come for another checkup and things like that. And I also had to go for psychiatric checkups, and I did that on some occasions when I went to see the orthopedic surgeon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony you mentioned that both in Visegrad and in Uzice you had x-rays made of your left leg. Do you have in your possession any of those x-rays, or did you have them in your possession?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had all those x-rays. There could have been 10 or 15 of them altogether. And I also had the x-rays of 1992 and 1993. I had it all wrapped and I had it all at home, but at home those things that we did not need, I mean old clothes, old footwear, everything that you didn't need much, we took to the new house. And when we were to get it ready, my wife and my daughter and I simply discarded all sorts of things we thought we did not need. Whether I threw away those x-rays, I don't know. Both my wife and I looked, and I asked my wife once again to go through every nook and cranny in that house to find them and she can't. Whether I threw it away, whether my wife did it, my daughter, I simply do not remember what I did with them. And I had all the x-rays from before and from every checkup. I must have had not less than ten x-rays -- no, surely more, and back to 1993. It was all wrapped, rolled up and wrapped, but I have simply no idea what I did with them, because whenever I went for a checkup, I had to take an x-ray and then go to see the doctor. That's why I had all of those x-rays. I also had the x-rays when I had surgery on my spine, and all that. How it happened that I do not have a single x-ray any more, beats me. Perhaps they are somewhere. I don't know. I asked my wife to go all over the house, in the attic and all over the place, but she simply has not found them yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the x-rays of the -- spinal x-rays. When was that, and did it have to do with some treatment or what?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suffered back pain from March 1994, March 1994, that is, I did feel that before that, but in March 1994 I could barely walk. I was practically bent to the ground. So that I went for treatment to the Visegrad spa, Visegradska Banja, but nothing helped. I spent 21 days there. And I went for checkups to a neurosurgeon, I knew the neurosurgeon, Dr. Davidovic, a good old surgeon. He said that I would have to have it operated, that I had a herniated disk. So that in June, they sent me to the Zemun hospital in Belgrade, to their neurosurgery, and they did x-rays and all the checkups and then I had my spine operated in Zemun. If I remember correctly, it was the doctor Radomir Vujovic who did the operation. I spent nine days there. I think so. Yes, nine days or something like that. And then they transferred me to the rehabilitation ward, that is, the same hospital, the Zemun hospital, but to their rehabilitation section, and I stayed there -- or, rather, I had to stay 30 work days for exercises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine, fine. That is enough. You've told us enough about that. Let us not waste time. So that was 1994. Will you now please explain to me, in 1992, when you left the hospital, do you remember for -- did you say that you were disabled and unfit to work and serve the army, and for how long; that is, when is it that you were called up for the first time after that injury?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that injury, 1992, until the very end of March 1993, I was on a sick-leave. And it was the very end of March, there was still snow on those mountains around, and I was assigned to the village of Rujiste. And I was there, attached to the command with elderly people, with sick people, those who could not move about; that is, we were not assigned any particularly heavy tasks. There was a Susnjar with me. He had also broken a leg, and we were together. He had fallen off his motorbike or something. And I stayed there for about 15 to 20 days. Then they transferred me to the village of Paocici, about two or three kilometres towards the Drina for about ten days. And then from Paocici, I went to my village, to Djurevici. And then I stayed there until the 6th of May, 1993, because that is my father's family's saint day, St. George, so that my wife and children came from Visegrad so that we could mark the holiday together. And that afternoon, when they were off to Visegrad, I went to see them off and I break my leg again on 6th of May, 1993. I slipped in the meadow and broke it again. So that in 1993, I once again -- that is, a driver came. It was some -- I'd say, well, 20 kilometres, yes, about as many, to Visegrad -- from Visegrad. So a driver came, took me to Visegrad, took the x-ray and decided it was another fracture, so once again to hospital in Uzice, and I was admitted by Dr. --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Fine, fine. Mr. Vasiljevic, we don't have to go that far because that is not the period that we are concerned with. But what I would like to know, however, is your knowledge of weapons and use of weapons. At the time when you were with the army in 1973, 1974, what kind of a weapon were you issued with and practiced shooting?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the quartermaster service and was issued with a rifle 48, that is, M-48, and the soldiers in my company, a company with three platoons, that is what we had, the kind of weapons that we had, so that we were not issued with anything special because we did not have any better weapons since we were quartermasters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that rifle, M-48, it is a rather old model, it is not a semi-automatic or automatic rifle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you yourself said that in 1992 you were issued with an automatic rifle for awhile.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone train you to use that rifle?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well nobody coached me. I mean they tell you how you fire individual shots or rounds of fire. It's not particularly difficult to grasp that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever suffer any incident? Were you ever injured by the weapon?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us in a few words.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, on the front line in Kladanj, that is, not exactly -- no, no, no, it's a place called Slivanj, I was on guard duty from 4.00 to 6.00. And as the day began to break and those three men who were with me were to get up, I was about to put a pot to make some coffee. And the rifle of one Nevenko Bozic, he had left his rifle there under a tree, and the snow was thawing and it was dripping and I asked, "Whose rifle is that?" and he said, "Mine," and he said, "It's cocked." He said, "Well, you can remove it." So I thought I would do it. And I folded the butt and I was to hang it on a tree, but then it fired off and wounded me, so that I was transferred that morning to Sokolac, to the hospital there, and I spent about 20 days or so there. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, apart from that shot when you wounded yourself in the leg, and what you were trained to do in the army, during those years, 1992, 1993, or later, did you ever fire a weapon?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I fire a weapon? Well, not really. Perhaps come Christmas and perhaps I would do it on -- or on the front line when you wanted to clean your weapon, then you usually have to fire a round. But I never took part in any operations or anything. I was breaking my leg. I couldn't run. And it happened twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, your last question incorporated something which was not in the previous answer. It may or may not be important. But you said, "Apart from that shot when you wounded yourself in the leg ..." Now, if you want to get that into evidence, you haven't got it into evidence yet, and may I suggest that you do it with a nonleading question if you do want to get it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The accused said he hurt his finger, but I understood that it was a toe.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In our language one uses the same word for both fingers and toes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, will you please clarify, did you hurt your finger or a toe?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: A toe, a toe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I should have asked that earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was important or not, but it just wasn't there in evidence, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you knew well somebody called Stanko Pecikoza.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Stanko his proper first name, or is it what you called him; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know him to be Stanko. I worked for him because he had a sawmill. I mean, I wasn't his proper worker. But after work, when I was building my house, I would go there to his storage space to get some timber and that. Stanko, well, I don't know, perhaps he was Stanimir and Stanko was for short. But I know him as Stanko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I show you his death certificate, a certificate, and then perhaps you can tell us whether that's the person you mean on the basis of the particulars in those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have Defence Exhibit D17 or 18. They are both in English. I have both these documents, D17-1 and D18-1 in B/C/S. And could these documents be shown to the witness, please -- to the accused, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you call it a Defence exhibit, it's not an exhibit. It's obviously a document you've numbered 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So is that the man that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pecikoza what?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanimir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this death certificate says that his name is the accused Stanimir?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the name of his mother and father and his wife is correct. And I also know his daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to tender this into evidence, two documents, that is, the death certificate of Stanimir Pecikoza, D17 in English, and D17-1 in B/C/S, and D18 which is the doctor's -- the coroner's finding which says Stanimir, Stanko, that is the document D18 in English, and D18-1 is the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Groome? Have you got copies of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We received them yesterday, and I didn't bring mine to court, but it's no fault of Mr. Domazet. Your Honour, just looking on the ELMO, I'd ask for some clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please slow down for the interpreters. Will you slow down, please, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry. Is this document a photocopy of the original document? I see the date of September 2001 handwritten on the bottom of it. Can we have some clarification as to how this document came to be created?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What's the point of all of this? Why do you need to prove his death, Mr. Domazet? Is it to explain why you can't call him as a witness, or is it to prove the date of his death?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Yes, the date of death is here. It is true that this death certificate in Visegrad was issued on the 27th of September, 1992, and these are photocopies -- 2001, excuse me. And the coroner's report is the report of the army authorities showing that Pecikoza -- Stanko Pecikoza was killed on the 20th of June, 1992, and we only have the photocopy of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But Mr. Groome has drawn the attention of the date on the bottom of the death certificate itself which is a date in 2001, which sounds as if it's just been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you let me explain. Up on the top there is the registration number and when the death was noted. And it says it was of 1992. And at the bottom of the paper, we have the date when the death certificate is issued, not the original. This is when it was requested and issued. So that down there we have the number of the application, which is 04, and so on and so forth, and the date when this certificate was issued. But above, under the number 24, and the year 1992, is when it was in the register of deaths, when it was recorded in the register of deaths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is this the explanation that anybody can go along and purchase or obtain a death certificate which is taken -- copied from the register and dated the date that it is issued. If that's the practice in the former Yugoslavia, then I don't see any problem with that. Most people get a death certificate, and once it's issued they keep a copy of it. But you got it for the purposes of getting evidence; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour, for another person who was killed meanwhile. You will see an identical document issued on the same day. Of course, it is a different person and a different date of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, Mr. Groome, it's a simple enough explanation, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no objection to the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. They will be Exhibits D17, 17.1; D18 and 18.1. Have you got copies for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: A copy for the exhibit itself and a copy for each of the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in English and in ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We don't have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The English version is -- you must have the English version. I give you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just wait for the court deputy to sort it out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have extra B/C/S copies here but no English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You must have an English, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We have lots of B/C/S versions, apparently, but no English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think that you have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we have them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, did you know the person by the name of Mitar Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you know him, and how was it that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is from the area of Zupa by origin, not very far from my village, some ten kilometres away, and he used to have a house in the vicinity of Prelovo, towards the village of Omar, I think, or Stari Grad. I don't remember the name of this hamlet. I didn't have much to do with him. He spent two years working in Dubrovnik, and once the war started he came back to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about what he did during the war?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard things. I heard that he was in Lukic's group and that he did all kinds of things, that he committed atrocities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He bore the same name as you do. Was there any other individual in Visegrad and around Visegrad with the same name and surname -- with the same name?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Mitar is not a very common name. I know maybe four or five Mitars in Visegrad, all generations included. It's a rather rare name, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am now going to show you a piece of paper that refers to him, but let me ask you first of all if that individual is still alive.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you now the death certificate for Mitar Knezevic so that you can tell us whether that was the individual that you just described.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is this the Mitar Knezevic whom you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to tender the death certificate for Mitar Knezevic into evidence, D16 in the English version and D16-1 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. They will be Exhibits D16 and D16.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is one more individual that I would like to discuss. You mentioned your cousin, Zeljko Sikiric, who was killed, and you described his funeral. I should now like to ask you to have a look at his death certificate and also the certificate which was issued by the local monastery and concerns his funeral, his burial. And you can please tell us whether that is, indeed, the individual whom you spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The death certificate should be D19 and the certificate issued by the monastery, D14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just take a look at these documents. I haven't seen these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. We've got 19, and now 14.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. They will be Exhibits D14, 14.1, and D19, 19.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, when you testify about the event which took place in Sase on the 7th of June, and your visit there, I should like to know, up until the 14th of June, did you happen to see the person by the name of Milan Lukic; that is, between the 7th of June, which you testified about, until the 14th of June, 1992, during that period of time, did you, at any point in time, see Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite remember. I probably did, but I didn't have any contact with him until the 14th of June. I no longer had anything to do with him, because I had witnessed what he had done and I simply could not -- no longer have any contact with him. I would probably see him pass by in the street in his car or something like that, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you allow for the possibility that you did see him in passing in his car, but your testimony is that you did not have any contact with him during that period of time; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you - at any point in time - until your arrest, hear about any survivors of the killing in Sase that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when it was that you heard about that, and from whom?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I heard about that in 1994 or 1995 from Milomir Obradovic, called Mica, who was captured in Gorazde and spent some time in captivity, a year or a year and a half, I don't know exactly how long. He is a colleague of mine, he's also a waiter by occupation, and he used to be my boss.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he told me that while he was being held prisoner, that one of the survivors told him about the incident in Sase, that Lukic had picked them up together with these two other individuals and that they were taken there to be executed, and that I too was present there. He didn't say anything about my participation in it, nothing of that sort, but I said that I was there. And I also mentioned the individual by the name of Meho Dzafic, whom I already spoke about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you which one of the survivors told him that story? I don't want you to use the name of the individual, but have a look at the list with pseudonyms.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but the other day in the Detention Unit, the guards took the document because apparently someone had called them from the Registry, because I had taken the list of witnesses together with me in the Detention Unit, and the guard came to my cell and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You'll be given a copy, Mr. Vasiljevic. Has that got the numbers 3 and 4 written against the two names on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. For the record, that's P164.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That was a copy of Exhibit P164.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Witness 32, VG032.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Obradovic told you that it was Witness VG032 who had told him about that incident?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period of time leading up to your arrest, did you ever hear through the media that that incident was being talked about, or any other event in which you allegedly took part? Did you hear anything about that from the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, I happened to receive a tape, an audiotape, which contained a recording of a radio broadcast, radio programme, and I remember that something was being said to the effect that Milan Lukic had brought five Muslims to the Visegrad spa, that they spent five or six days there, that he had taken their gold and money, and that he bit an individual by the surname of Sisic so hard that his eyes fell out of their sockets. So that was the first thing. And then there's something about another individual whose name I don't want to mention because he's probably a Prosecution witness, but I can write down his name -- I'm Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sorry, actually, I haven't finished the first one. And then they were apparently released by one of our Serb neighbours, but the name of that neighbour was not mentioned. And then there was this other story which was told by a witness who testified here in public - I can mention his name - Ferid Spahic, that they had been victims of the events in Rogatica, and he went on to mention names of two individuals from Visegrad, the name of two Serbs who apparently carried out the execution. And then they went on to say that another mass crime had occurred in the village of Bikovac, in which incident Momir Savic, Zoran Sekulic, and Mitar [Realtime transcript read in error "Mito"] Vasiljevic, forced a large number of Muslims into a house which they subsequently set on fire, and the incident resulted in their deaths, all of them, with only one who survived the incident. So the overall story was told by the journalist, but the specific descriptions were given by the witnesses. And I felt terrible, I panicked, because I knew that it was not me, especially because I never had anything to do with Momir Savic or Sekulic. I don't know what Savic was. I think he was some kind of local commander in his area. But I never had anything to do with them. But anyway, that's what I heard on that tape, and then later on I heard from some other people that the person who survived the incident at Bikovac underwent treatment in France, and that he -- and that the survivor gave a statement on TV in which the name of Milan Lukic was mentioned together with his men, and I wanted to know whether she mentioned me and he said no. And I felt relieved because the story was told by the survivor of the incident. Later on, perhaps in 1967 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says the witness.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a book was published about the incidents, the events in Visegrad, and this survivor again spoke about those events and she mentioned that particular group but did not mention me once again. So again I must say that I felt a certain relief because, after all, it was a survivor of the incident and my name was not mentioned in the story of that survivor. So I simply put that problem away. I really felt relieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, the transcript has recorded the witness as saying Mico Vasiljevic rather than Mitar Vasiljevic, but I think it's clear from his answer that he thought his own name had been used. This was about the other house burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We wish to note that there's no way of knowing whether the survivor is a woman or a man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you mentioned a year when this book was published. It simply cannot be 1967. Can you remember the year when it was published?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what I said. 1996 or 1997.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The record read 1967, which is impossible.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you said that you heard from this person by the surname of Obradovic about this witness story, and you also heard from others that your name was mentioned in that context. Did you ever -- did it ever occur to you that you might be arrested and taken to court?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I know that I did not have a weapon, that I had already returned my weapon before the incident in Sase. I had no knowledge whatsoever about Pionirska Street until I arrived here in The Hague, I didn't know I was charged with it. I also know that I was not present at Bikovac. I mean, why, for example, would I ever rent a house to the French members of SFOR if I had been involved in such incidents? I mean, I would never dare do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you live in Vojvoda Stepe Street in Visegrad throughout that period of time, or did you absent yourself from the town of Visegrad for a longer period of time, or not?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Vojvoda Stepe Street for the past 20 years. More than 20, 25 actually, from 1976 or thereabouts, and I never left that house. I was never away for any longer period of time, except for the time that I spent in hospitals. And when I finished my treatments, only during those periods of time when I was at the front line, that would have been, like, seven days at most, I never worked outside Visegrad, nor did I ever work abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For throughout that period you lived and you worked in Visegrad, and you resided at the address you indicated?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you rent out your house to the members of the French SFOR under your name and surname?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did they know your identity? Did they know that your name was Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was stated in the contract. That was the contract that actually I received from them, the layout of the contract. And not only my name and surname, everything was there, all the details, the rent and other terms and conditions which are normally found in a contract like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they lived during that period of time next the house where you lived in?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They lived in my house and I lived in this other house that I told you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they arrived on the 14th of July, 1999, until I was arrested on the 25th of January, 2000. It was not only one group of soldiers. There were, like, three groups or three shifts, each consisting of seven soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you see them from time to time? Did you have any contact with them?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say them on a daily basis. I mean, the house is, after all, only 6 or 7 metres away. Sometimes my wife would cook something for them. They would buy things. And they were really very fair and correct. They would also invite us over to their place, and they were always very considerate with my children. They would buy little things for them. And I often went to the town with them. And then when this -- when a new group arrived, they always wanted to know where the best restaurants were, where they can have a good meal, so they always wanted me to accompany them on the first day. Sometimes we would go together to the swimming pool. And on the eve of my arrest, on the 24th of January, they were in my house, they spent the evening at my place. We were together all the time. Sometimes it was difficult for us to understand each other, but they had a little dictionary. And I would accompany them to the local shop and I would help them with the language. It's not that I could speak any French, but they had this little dictionary and I -- so I was able to talk to them. My daughter speaks some English, not very much, but she could say a few words in English to them. Yes, I saw them every day. We were living in two houses which were right next to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, could you tell us, but very briefly, something about your arrest. Under what circumstances did it take place?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested in the new house. I was on my way back from the town and they were in this vehicle, and I said but did they want to -- if they were going there to my house. So they stop and they gave me a ride. And then when we got home, one of the soldiers said that the central heating was not okay. But it was not actually the central heating, but we called it that way. It was some kind of stove. So apparently there was a problem with it, so I wanted to -- went out to check the electricity. I didn't know what the problem was, and I had to do something because they didn't have any heating. So I was thinking of what I should do. And then as I went upstairs, I just saw a number of soldiers wearing masks, and they put this hood on my head and some kind of ear stops in my ears. They tied me down and put it on a stretcher, I don't know what it was, exactly, and then they took me to a vehicle and transported me. I actually couldn't see any of the soldiers who arrested me. I cannot tell you who they were. They were wearing those masks. I don't know. I don't even know how many there were. Maybe there were some other soldiers. I don't know. They were wearing those caps, those hoods on their heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you didn't know about the proceedings, and you were arrested on the basis of a secret indictment. Had you known that an investigation had been initiated against you, would you have responded to the summons?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have, of course, responded to the summons. And if I had known about the charges, that is, the house at Bikovac and in Pionirska Street, I would have talked to those soldiers about it, because I had the relevant medical documentation, I would have asked those people, those soldiers who were at my house, who to contact, because I would have tried to establish contact with relevant authorities. I would have shown them what I had. Of course, I wasn't going to spend my whole life in hiding. Lukic, for example, he can spend the rest of his life in hiding, but it's a shame. I mean, I'm here in detention, and this person killed all those women and children. I really feel terribly, terribly embarrassed. I feel so sorry for the families of those people. I mean, after all, they were children and women. I mean, there's nothing I can do about it. I had nothing to do with it. I just keep hoping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, I have only two or three very brief questions for you. Did you ever have a moustache?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the nickname of Mrkela tell you anything? Have you ever heard of an individual with a nickname like that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was in my neighbourhood a person by the nickname of Mrkela. He was killed in war. He was younger than me. Dusko, Dusko Ranac, I think, was his name. His house was a little bit further from my place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear people say that you were known under that nickname, and that it was under that nickname that you participated in certain actions?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic, called Mrkela? No, no one ever called me that way. There was a very famous football player from the Red Star club from Belgrade who was called Mitar Mrkela, so maybe that was sometimes used as a joke. No, I was never called Mrkela. I just knew this individual by the nickname of Mrkela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vasiljevic, you never had the nickname Mrkela, you were never known under that nickname?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. Thank you, Your Honour. This concludes my examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I just ask that the ELMO be shifted a little bit. I'm unable to see Mr. Vasiljevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, the first thing I'd ask you to do this morning is to take a look at that document in front of you, P164. A number of those people have come to court and have testified that they recognised you and in fact pointed you out here in the courtroom. My question to you is: When some of those people came into the courtroom, did you recognise any of them by name? So did any of those people enter into the courtroom and you immediately recognised them and you knew their name? Can you look down that list and tell us, were there any such people like that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to indicate who they were by using the number.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I'll tell you about the persons who did not seek protection. I know Poljo, Suad, and Ferid Spahic, I know them. I'll go just down the list. VG32, VG55, 59, 61, 87, 115. 014, had somebody asked me about his name before, I wouldn't have known him. I mean, I knew him by sight. And this one here, he testified in public, this one here, let me just check it, I don't want to go wrong there -- no, perhaps I'm not sure, so I shouldn't read out his name. The witness who testified about Zepa, I think he testified in public. I think his name is [redacted]. I know him too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, aside from these people now who you have indicated you knew them by name when they entered the courtroom, I think you mentioned that VG14, you didn't know his name until he entered the courtroom. Are there other people on this list whom you recognised as having seen in Visegrad or perhaps in the restaurant but you did not know their name when they entered this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned 014, and I see that from 014's statement. But had I come across him somewhere, had I met him, I wouldn't have known his either first or last name. I remember his face, though. 013; 018, no, I wouldn't -- I wouldn't have been able; 38 especially, because it's a child; 55, 59, yes, I would; 61, yes, I would, I always remember him; 77, no, I don't think would have remembered him; 78, likewise -- oh, no, sorry; 081, I don't know if I told you that I had known him. I did know her. Well, she was practically a former neighbour, about a kilometre away. I don't know if I mentioned her as having known her. Then 84, 87, yes, I did recognise that person, even though it was by videolink; 101, no; 105, no; 115, yes, I would have recognised that person, and I also met him in the street somewhere; and this one, 014, yes, I would have recognised him, but I wouldn't have known his name, either first or last.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, let me ask you some questions in particular regarding some of these people. Let us first go down to VG81. You just told us that you lived about a kilometre away from this particular person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she lived -- no, as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without telling us where she lived specifically, please. Without telling us where she lived specifically, can you give us an idea of approximately how many years you knew VG81?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew her for a long time. I knew her -- well, I wouldn't know exactly how long, but it was long, because I was a waiter and she worked somewhere, I won't mention where, and they used to come there, they had their meals there. So I know her very well. I know her brother, I know what her brother's name is. [redacted] [redacted]. But she lived somewhere in the town. Whereabouts in the town, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the times that she would come into your restaurant, would it be fair to say that you would have normal conversation with her?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, she would be a patron there. They would have their breakfast or they would have their brunch there. But not only -- that was not the only way that I knew her. I knew her from around the town. I know her well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to estimate that or agree with me that during the course of the years you had an opportunity to see her over 100 times?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not a hundred times. Well, not as many. But there's no need to, because I didn't always work in one place. That particular restaurant was near the municipal hall. When I worked at the Visegrad hotel, they didn't come to have their breakfast there, or in the Visegrad spa. But I know her well enough, and I also know what her brother's name is, and I know where her brother works too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me now ask you about VG84. The transcript is a bit unclear on this person. Did you know this person, or did you recognise this person when VG84 entered the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am correct, it is the person -- no, let me see. How shall I put it, the person who was born in 1988, isn't it? So it's a child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just to clarify, did you recognise this person when VG84 entered the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a child far removed from me, and he came from a village somewhere. No, I didn't know him when he was a child. I never knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, VG87, can you give us an idea of how long you knew VG87?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him well too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many years have you known VG87?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've known him as a child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say, during the course of the years that you have known him, that you have spoken to him on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, VG115, again, can you give us an idea of how long you've known this person?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know how long. That person comes from a town; I won't mention which one. I know that she was married to a man -- or, rather, she married and she came with him to Visegrad, and then she remarried, and her first husband came from my area. I know that she -- that she worked for a company. Whether I ever communicated with her in any way particularly, no, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea of approximately how many years you know this person, or perhaps the year that you first came to know this person?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I can tell you is that I didn't know what she was called. I know her as an individual. When? When she arrived and when she came to live in Visegrad, I wouldn't really be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be more than five years?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could be, thereabouts. Well, she married, and, well, if we take 1992, yes, could be. Could be longer than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be as many as ten years?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's at least five years; you would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I knew her by sight from around the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, during the course of my questions to you, I will ask you for certain information. During the course of your statement, you indicated some fear for your family at mentioning certain individuals. My intent is not to jeopardise your wife or your children or your family, so if I ask you a question that you feel the answer does maybe perhaps cause some jeopardy to your family, I'd ask you to tell the Court so that we may deal with it; is that understood?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I want to ask you once again, you and Their Honours, when we speak about persons, not to do it in public. I won't mention -- I won't mention those persons, because I have a child at the university, a brother is in Belgrade, and a sister. So if you could phrase it in some other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are there other names that we can add to the list that you've put at the foot of Exhibit 164?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Those are the only two names that he expressed concern regarding in the statement. There may be more, and perhaps he can advise the court about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, the best way of dealing with this will be, if you don't want a particular name referred to, you better make a list of them sometime when you have a moment, so that we all know those are the names you do not want mentioned. Are you able to do that during the short adjournment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will not get into any area that would require him to mention those names before the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk to you or ask you a few more questions regarding this relationship called kum in Serbian culture. You told us on Tuesday that your father was the godfather of Milan Lukic and Milan Lukic's brother and sister; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, let me try and explain it to you. What I said was that he was Milan Lukic's and his brother's and sister's godfather, but we are related as kums. I think I said he was the godfather. Yes, he was their godfather. So kum, that is kum, and Milan's father was -- my grandfather, for instance, was the godfather of Milan's father, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Serbian culture, would a godfather have a life-long commitment to protect his godchildren, to advise them, to counsel them? Would that be a life-long commitment to his godchildren?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is his lifetime commitment to christen, to be the best man at weddings. Well, it is not a commitment, but it is said that it is a sin to break up that relationship, and it happens very seldom that this kind of relationship is broken. You go and you christen somebody's child, and I know of cases when the man arrived from Australia to be the godfather or godmother, so that -- because it is important. If, for instance, the presumed godfather falls ill or something, then people will wait for him to get well in order to perform the ritual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your children, who was the godfather of your two children?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: My children, I've told you that all members of the Vasiljevic and Lukics are mixed -- involved together; that is, Milan Lukic or his brothers could not christen my children, could not be godfathers to my children. My children's godfather was Luka Lukic. My daughter's godmother was his mother, and my daughter, by Luka Lukic, and I couldn't be the godfather of Luka Lukic's son, for instance, I couldn't do that, because he was my -- he is my godfather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does Milan Lukic have children, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has a little daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you involved in the baptism of his daughter?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was her godfather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are the godfather of Milan Lukic's daughter?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how old would she be today?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, four or five maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that would mean that she would have been baptised in 1996, around that time?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think she was already two or two and a half when she was baptised. 1998 or was it 1997, I'm not sure. Either 1997 or 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in your testimony on Tuesday that this relationship, members of a kum would also participate in each other's weddings; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. Weddings, family saints, that is, Slavas, they were -- they are there. Funerals too, of course, they are bound to attend --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate --

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- funerals, if they are there, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in -- sorry. Did Milan Lukic participate in your wedding?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he couldn't do that, he couldn't be my best man. Luka Lukic was my best man, again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he present at your wedding?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Milan Lukic married?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you attend his wedding?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was his best man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were Milan Lukic's best man at his wedding?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was he married?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1995 or 1996, one of those two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He wasn't married in the summer of 1992, was he?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned about funerals, and I think you said that members of kum are bound to attend funerals in the other family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just add. Well, I mean, yes, it is your duty, but if you cannot come, if you are prevented from attending, then of course you don't. But that is how it should be done. If you are there, if you are present, if you are available, it would be really a disgrace if you didn't attend the funeral. Now, say, if I'm in Belgrade, to attend a funeral in Visegrad, well, no, not in that case. But to be a kum at the wedding or be at the baptism, that is, to have the godfather or the godmother or the best man, no, that is a confirm commitment then, otherwise he'd have to wait. For instance, if I'm ill, if I'm in hospital, then he would have to wait for me to get well and come there to do that. He cannot pick up another kum, that is, a best man or the godfather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, between 1992 and the time of your arrest, were there funerals either in your family or the Lukic family that you attended and that Milan Lukic was also present?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Nobody died in my family, and I think nobody died in his either. No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a hypothetical question to maybe understand this kum relationship a little bit better, and the question would be: If your wife and Milan Lukic's wife didn't like each other or had an argument, would that affect the bond of kumship between yourself and Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: To break it, you mean? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Would it break it?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, it wouldn't, no. No. We'd have to resolve it somehow, to see whose mistake it was, whose responsibility it was. But that kind of relationship would not be called into question, oh, no. No way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the relationship between two men that are in kumship would be as strong as the bond between two brothers?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, dear, let me see how to put it. Well, with a brother you communicate like a brother. But I think -- I mean, if brother asks you for a favour and you're against it or you say no, I won't do it for you, or if -- for instance, if you will serve a better meal to your brother or to your kum, it is the latter one who will get it. So if, for instance, you can choose between two types of a meal, then you'll give the better one to your kum rather than your brother. And the question who you are more -- who you are fonder of, well, that's another story. But, you know, a brother is a brother, after all. So a kum is not a blood relation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this would be a good place to take the morning break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just been handed a sheet of paper with the names that the accused wishes not to mention publicly, so perhaps we can deal with how the Court would like us to handle this matter at this stage. It's a list of 19 different names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I suggest we proceed with the numbering system that we've started on Exhibit P164. So we'll start at the top and we'll call that first one VGD5 and go down the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll just point out that number 7 has already been assigned a number, VGD4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sorry, number 7, is that the same -- same given name?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it's the same person. We can, of course, inquire of Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see. He's written it beside it. I'm sorry. VGD4. Is that the only one that's already been given a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour. I'm sorry. I had this name misspelled. Number 6 has already been given a number, VGD3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: VGD3. Well, now, if everybody has their sheet in front of them, the first name will be VGD5; the second name is VGD6; the third name is VGD7; the fourth name is VGD8; the fifth name is VGD9; the sixth name is VGD3; the seventh name is VGD4; the eighth name is VGD10; the ninth is VGD11; the tenth is VGD12; the eleventh is VGD13; the twelfth is VGD14; the thirteenth is VGD15; the fourteenth is VGD16; the fifteenth is VGD17; the sixteenth is VGD18; the seventeenth is VGD19; the eighteenth is VGD20; and the last name, the nineteenth is VGD21. Now, that document will be Exhibit D -- Mr. Domazet, you've started to use numbers, obviously. What's your next free number?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Number 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be Exhibit D22, and it will be under seal. Number 22 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one other thing. I'm sure the Court is already aware, one of these people is an indictee in this case. I'm not sure how it will be possible to discuss him without -- I'm not sure that the number will give the protection that is sought. Would the Court want me to pause before I ask questions regarding that person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Normally one wouldn't worry, but I suppose the accused's concern is what he may be seen to be revealing in relation to that person, so it would be just as well if we can avoid dealing with him until you have raised it specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that the ELMO be adjusted again so that I can see the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, we ended the first session this morning with you using a metaphor of the kum would get a better meal than the brother. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take by your answer that the relationship between the kum is even stronger than that of between two brothers?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's not what I meant. It implies a certain respect for the relationship of kum, but one cannot say that that relationship is stronger than the relationship with one's brother, no. A brother is always a brother, of course. It's just that I -- it would be out of respect that I would serve my kum in a better way, that I would give him a better bed in my house. For example, if both of them were my house guests, my brother and my kum, I would probably give my kum a better bed because your brother would always forgive you if you're not on a certain level. But you have to treat your kum with a certain amount of respect. It's not that your relationship with him is stronger than your relationship with your brother. Of course, a brother is always a brother. You can complain to your brother if you have problems, but you should not, for example, explain to your kum in you're lacking something. You would always turn to your brother first, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a brother?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would he have --

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: One brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would he also be considered a kum of Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but he is his kum, regardless of the fact that I was his best man and I christened his child. That doesn't really matter. It could have been my brother. It would not constitute any serious, I don't know, violation of the tradition, no. It all stays in the family. It's all one and the same relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you estimate for us how many different men would be in a similar relationship of kumship to Milan Lukic? Not an exact number, but just give us an estimate.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you mean. For example, are you asking me whether I can have other kums except for Milan Lukic, is that what you have in mind, or whether he can have other people as his kums from some other family, not only from the Vasiljevic family? Yes, they can have three or four kums all bearing different surnames. At the same time you can act as a kum to a member of a different family. That has nothing to do with that. I mean, I can have this type of relationship with ten different families. But I have to tell you that I probably wouldn't accept if someone called me to act as his kum just because his other traditional kum is someone he's having problems with, if he had some kind of quarrel with him or things like that. In that case, I wouldn't accept. But usually, in most of the cases, it's a very long-standing tradition within each family. I don't know in my family how old this relationship is, probably over a hundred years old, and it was never broken in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me state the question again. If Milan Lukic were here and he were to be asked, how many different kums do you have, can you tell us how many different men could you name, approximately, that Milan Lukic would say, these are my kum? Is it five? Is it ten? Is it 15? Can you estimate for us, please?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, all Vasiljevic families are his kums. It's just that he cannot be a godfather to every child from that family. One always knows exactly whose godfather or best man you can be. For example, Milan Lukic cannot be my best man, he couldn't have christened my children, but I can do that to him. In my case, it was his cousin who was my best man and the godfather of my children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Vasiljevic family, how many men would be considered the kum of Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I suggest that you limit that question to those who could be his best man or to christen his child. Isn't that what you're trying to get to eventually? Because you've asked that question and he's given you the question. All men are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, in the Vasiljevic family, how many men were possible candidates to be Milan Lukic's best man?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can be his best man, my brother too, my uncle's sons, my father's brother's sons or daughters, no matter, but it usually involves male members of the family. So Milan Lukic's children, the children of his brother can be christened by myself, my brother, and my uncle's children. Not anyone else. If I had five uncles, then of course all of their children would be the candidates. But not my aunt's children, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people are you talking about now?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, the case we are talking about, four of us. I, my brother, and my two cousins, sons of my uncle, because they are the only two cousins that I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you personally aware of any other families, not Vasiljevics, who are in this special relationship with the Lukic family?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, no, I don't know of any specific families involving this type of relationship. Well, they probably have close links with other families as well, but they have their relatives, their in-laws, like myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, separate and apart from this relationship of kumship, Mr. Domazet asked you on Tuesday whether you socialised with Milan Lukic, and you told him that you did not, in part, because he is 13 years younger than you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, let me tell you, we didn't have an opportunity to socialise. I'm 13 years his senior. I was already employed; he was still a child. Once he completed his education, he was still very young. He was a child when I started to work. He completed his education, he did his military service, and then he left Visegrad. I don't know whether he went to Switzerland right away or spent some time working in Serbia. That I don't know. But anyway, he was absent and he didn't visit very often, so I didn't have much opportunity to socialise with him, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period between when he returned to Visegrad in 1992 and the 7th of June, 1992, did you socialise with him at any time during that period?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, he was in Switzerland. I didn't have opportunity to see him. Maybe he would come over on holidays, but I don't remember those days before the war. I don't remember seeing him or socialising with him in particular. He would be there for awhile on leave or on holiday, but he wouldn't stay very long. I don't know whether he had an apartment in Belgrade -- yes, yes, he did have an apartment in Belgrade before the war, but he would probably go to his family's house in his village when on holiday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there did come a time in May of 1992 that he did return to Visegrad from Switzerland; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the time between when he returned in May of 1992 and the 7th of June, did you socialise with him at any time in that period?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Socialise with him, well, I would see him on the street from time to time, but I didn't have any particular contacts with him, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then from the 7th of June to the 14th of June, you testified here this morning that you made a decision not to have any further contact with him because of what you observed him do on the 7th of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: How shall I put it? I was present there. I have already told the story, I can tell it to you again, but I simply tried to avoid him as much as possible because I too was afraid, despite the fact that he was my kum, that we were in this kum relationship, regardless of that fact, it was just very embarrassing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do admit that earlier today you did tell us that you simply could no longer have contact with Milan Lukic after the 7th of June; do you admit that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean if I saw him at all or ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, we were talking about whether you would socialise with him after the 7th of June and before the 14th of June, when you say you went into the hospital. During that period of time, in response to a question Mr. Domazet asked, you stated, "... I simply could not -- no longer have any contact with him." Do you remember saying that here this morning about an hour ago?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I said that. How can I explain this to you? It's just that I did not wish to have any contact with him. I didn't want to have any contact with him. It was just my natural impulse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us why you didn't want to have contact with him?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, it was because of the fact that I was present there, of how he behaved, of how heartless he was. I'm referring to the incident by the river. I was present there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've used the word embarrassed. Is the reason for not having contact with him because you were embarrassed to be seen with him because of what he did?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I really no longer felt like -- I mean, I christened his child and I was his best man because I had to do it. But ever since that time, it was very embarrassing for me to be in his company. Sometimes he had come over and we would have a drink, but I -- I couldn't wait to see him off. I mean, I really didn't feel like being with him. And when he was in prison, I never visited him there. I don't know how long he spent in prison, five or six months, but I never went there to see him, I never inquired about him, I wasn't interested in his situation at all. I never went to see him there. If I had had any respect left for him, I would have visited him in prison, but I never attempted to do that, I never inquired about him at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you felt this way, wouldn't it have been possible to ask one of the other four or five members of your family to be his best man, to be the godfather of his children? Wouldn't that have been a possibility?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, if he comes to see me and if he asks me, it's very difficult for me to refuse. I mean, he was the one who directly contacted me for that purpose. If he had gone to my brother or my cousin, it would have been also difficult for them to refuse the offer and to send him over to me, to Mitar. It would really have been a pity because of the children and because of other kums. It's not only that he would be offended, everybody else would have been offended and angry, and I would have probably been exposed to the criticism of my family. It's this kind -- it's -- it was my duty, my Christian duty. But he spent more time in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So of the four or five people that could have been his best man and the godfather of his children, did Milan Lukic ask any of those before he asked you, or were you the first person he asked of those people?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the first person he asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were in the hospital between the 14th and, I believe, the 28th of July. When you returned from the hospital, did you socialise with Milan Lukic at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time I still had my plaster on and I was on sick-leave and I was walking on crutches. So I spent most of the time at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the time that you came home from the hospital, you did not socialise with Milan Lukic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time, no, it was impossible for me to socialise. I was at home most of the time, all the time actually, except for my checkups, especially after my cast was taken off. I had to be very careful. The doctor's recommendation was that I was to move as little as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the remainder of 1992, did you ever socialise with Milan Lukic at all?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see him from time to time, but I cannot say that we socialised. It was getting winter time and I was still very ill. I didn't want to go out because of the road conditions. And it was until the end of March that I was on sick-leave. I don't know exactly when it was that he was arrested in 1993, whether it was in January or February. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to the 16th and 17th of November, 2000. Do you recall participating in an interview in this building, in the basement of this building?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Prosecutor? With you? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Myself and other members of the Office of the Prosecutor's staff?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that a voluntary statement?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before you gave that statement, were you advised of your right to the assistance of an attorney and an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, was Mr. Domazet present during the entire statement?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also advised that you did not have to answer any questions that were put to you? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you also advised that that statement could be used in evidence at trial?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after being advised of those rights, did you proceed with the interview? Did you give a voluntary statement?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic [Resumed]
